title: Harvest and Winter
premise: Pest controller Tamsin Iversen is called to Hollowmere Farm, where something has been leaving human fingerprints in flour, ash, and frost — prints that match her missing uncle's. Beneath the farmyard, an excavation crew unearths a cellar door sealed from the inside, and the workers who opened it begin to change: their memories rewritten, their bodies cooling toward the temperature of the soil. Tamsin learns that in 1974 her grandfather and his neighbors buried a man alive to steal his land, and the thing below has spent fifty years learning to wear his face. To survive the winter it is writing into their bones, she must return what was taken — the deed, the name, the truth — even if that means confessing her family's crime to the town and opening the door from the outside.
about_author: Felix Iversen is the pen name of a former rural surveyor who spent a decade documenting farmsteads across the northern counties, where he collected more local burial stories than soil samples. He writes horror about property lines, family ledgers, and the debts that outlive the people who incurred them.

chapters.title: The Call-Out
chapters.summary: Tamsin arrives at Hollowmere Farm to deal with what the owner swears is vermin, finding instead neat rows of small handprints pressed into pantry flour. POV: Tamsin. The beat is dry professional skepticism curdling into unease as she realizes the prints are human, adult-sized, and made by someone walking on the ceiling.

chapters.title: Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Tamsin dusts the prints, photographs them, and tells herself it's a prank by the farmhand — until she matches one against her own memory of her uncle Aldous's hands, missing since 1998. POV: Tamsin. Emotional beat: the first hairline crack in her unbelief, masked by irritation at her own sentimentality.

chapters.title: Hollowmere
chapters.summary: A portrait of the village: the farm's owner Mrs. Ellery, the excavation crew surveying for a new septic field, and the way locals go quiet when 1974 comes up. POV: rotating close-third through crew foreman Dev Chaudhary. Beat: normalcy established precisely so its collapse will hurt; Dev notices the ground over the yard stays unfrozen while everything around it frosts.

chapters.title: What the Ground Keeps
chapters.summary: The excavator bites into the yard and strikes not pipe but timber — a door, oak, iron-banded, lying flat like a lid. The hinges show no rust; the latch is thrown from beneath. POV: Dev. Beat: collective bravado as the crew jokes about cellars, undercut by the reader's knowledge of the seal.

chapters.title: Sealed From the Inside
chapters.summary: Against Tamsin's advice they cut the latch. Below: a stone chamber, a straw pallet, a bowl long since emptied, and walls scored with tally marks — thousands, far more than fifty years could hold. POV: Tamsin descending first because no one else will. Beat: dread arriving as arithmetic; the tallies don't add up and never will.

chapters.title: The First Cold Man
chapters.summary: Crew member Pete stops coming to work; when Tamsin visits, he sits in an unheated room, breathless, reciting harvest dates he couldn't know. His skin is cool as cellar stone. POV: Tamsin. Beat: horror shifts from place to person — the door was a mouth, and it has begun swallowing.

chapters.title: Ledger of 1974
chapters.summary: In the parish records office Tamsin finds the land transfer: Hollowmere passed from a man named Corwin Hale to her grandfather in October 1974, weeks after Hale 'left the district.' No death record. No forwarding address. POV: Tamsin. Beat: inheritance revealed as theft; grief and shame arrive together.

chapters.title: Mrs. Ellery Remembers
chapters.summary: The old owner, dying and past fear, tells Tamsin what the men did: a dispute over water rights, a night of cider, a cellar, a door nailed shut while Hale begged. She kept paying rent ever since, to whom she wouldn't say. POV: Mrs. Ellery. Beat: confession as contagion — telling the truth makes the cold spread faster.

chapters.title: Frost Patterns
chapters.summary: Windows across the village bloom with fern-like frost that isn't frost: under magnification it's script, repeating one phrase — RETURN WHAT WAS TAKEN. Pete dies sitting up, smiling, his body at soil temperature. POV: Dev. Beat: the haunting becomes public, communal, undeniable.

chapters.title: Aldous
chapters.summary: Tamsin finds her uncle's old letters in her mother's attic: Aldous investigated the same prints in 1998, got close to the truth, and wrote 'it wears him now' before vanishing. The last letter is addressed to her, though she was nine. POV: Tamsin. Beat: personal stakes fuse with historical ones; the family debt includes her.

chapters.title: The Second Crew
chapters.summary: Two more workers begin cooling; Dev, infected next, fights it by staying near fires that do nothing. He describes dreams of counting — endless tally marks, each one a day, each day a name. POV: Dev. Beat: body horror braided with memory horror; the thing doesn't kill, it replaces.

chapters.title: Wearing Him
chapters.summary: Tamsin sees it at last: a figure in the yard at dusk with her uncle's gait, her grandfather's coat, a face assembled from borrowed features and always slightly wrong. It waves. Politely. POV: Tamsin. Beat: terror tempered by terrible recognition — it wants to be claimed as family.

chapters.title: The Town That Buries Twice
chapters.summary: Tamsin takes the story to the village meeting; descendants of the other 1974 men deny everything until shown the frost-script, which spells their grandfathers' names. One old man breaks and admits there were four of them that night. POV: ensemble, anchored on Tamsin. Beat: justice outside the law begins — confession as the only currency the dead accept.

chapters.title: Four Names
chapters.summary: Research identifies all four perpetrators: her grandfather, the two other farmers, and — shockingly — the young constable who helped cover it up, whose badge number matches one scratched inside the cellar. POV: Tamsin. Beat: the law itself complicit; every institution meant to protect failed the man in the dark.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Tamsin compiles the restitution: the deed, the stolen wages found in her grandfather's strongbox, the constable's badge from an estate sale, and a written confession signed by the surviving families. The cold deepens; the thing grows more present, more patient, as if savoring. POV: Tamsin. Beat: grim purpose replacing fear — she is preparing a funeral fifty years late.

chapters.title: Dev's Last Warm Day
chapters.summary: Dev, nearly gone, asks Tamsin to read him the confession aloud; hearing the truth spoken slows his cooling, proof that acknowledgment matters to whatever holds them. He gives her his tally-dreams as a map: the chamber is bigger than the cellar, and the door is only its mouth. POV: Dev. Beat: tenderness inside horror; friendship as resistance.

chapters.title: The Door From the Outside
chapters.summary: Winter solstice eve. Tamsin descends with the relics and the confession, followed by the descendants carrying candles, and finds the chamber's far wall carved with a second door — this one sealed from the outside too, by hands in 1974. Something on the other side has been knocking politely for fifty years. POV: Tamsin. Beat: revelation reframes everything — they didn't bury one man; they locked away what he became.

chapters.title: Corwin Hale
chapters.summary: Tamsin reads the confession aloud at the threshold; the frost-script stills; the figure with the borrowed face kneels. When she speaks Hale's name and offers back the deed, the wrongness drains from it, leaving a gaunt man-shaped absence that steps toward the inner door. POV: Tamsin. Beat: climax as ceremony — naming, returning, witnessing; justice performed, not enforced.

chapters.title: Unsealed
chapters.summary: Together they break the inner seal. What emerges isn't Hale but everything the winter took: the cold leaves the villagers' bodies, the tallies finish themselves, and the chamber collapses into clean, ordinary earth. The figure with her uncle's face looks at Tamsin once — with Aldous's eyes, briefly kind — and goes. POV: Tamsin. Beat: catharsis shadowed by cost; some things return only by leaving.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Dev recovers warmth slowly, keeping a fire lit for months out of habit. The village records the confession publicly; the Hale family, traced to distant survivors, receives the land's value. Frost stops writing. POV: rotating. Beat: quiet repair — justice outside the law proving slower but truer than any court.

chapters.title: The New Deed
chapters.summary: Tamsin transfers Hollowmere to a land trust in Corwin Hale's name and plants the yard where the door was. Digging, she finds nothing but soil — and one small object: her uncle's pocket watch, running again, set to the hour of his disappearance. POV: Tamsin. Beat: inheritance redeemed; memory honored rather than buried.

chapters.title: First Frost
chapters.summary: A year later, the season's first frost writes ordinary ferns on ordinary windows. Tamsin keeps pest-controlling, keeps believing nothing — except that she checks every sealed space she enters, and always knocks once, politely, before opening anything shut from the inside. POV: Tamsin. Beat: resolution with a scarred edge; belief redefined as vigilance, memory as a door left respectfully ajar.
